content.text: In all programming languages, managing memory efficiently is crucial. If unused memory is not deallocated, it can lead to memory shortages and errors like "Out of Memory."
Java divides memory into two main regions for memory allocation:

In Java, memory deallocation is handled by the Garbage Collector. It automatically frees memory occupied by objects that are no longer in use. Objects are eligible for garbage collection under the following conditions:

items: When a reference is set to null: The object is no longer referenced, making it eligible for garbage collection.
When a reference is reassigned to a new object: If no references point to the original object, it is eligible for garbage collection.

When a reference is local to a method: After the method finishes execution, the reference is removed from the stack, and if the reference pointed to an object, that object becomes eligible for garbage collection.

content.text: The finalize() method allows you to define specific actions to perform before an object is garbage collected. This method is invoked just before an object is destroyed, allowing for cleanup operations.

content.text: Thus, two objects are eligible for garbage collection after line 4.
In Java, variables have three main scopes:

items: Instance Variables: These belong to an object and are stored in the heap memory. They are deallocated when the object is garbage collected.
Local Variables: These are created within methods or blocks and are deallocated when the method or block finishes execution.
Static Variables: These belong to the class and are shared across all instances. They exist as long as the class is loaded in memory.

sections.heading: Best Practices for Efficient Memory Management

items: Always nullify references to objects that are no longer needed to help the garbage collector identify unreferenced objects.
Avoid unnecessary memory usage by limiting the lifetime of variables.
Use finalize() when necessary, but it is not a reliable mechanism for resource management in modern Java development.

content.text: By understanding these memory management principles, you can write more efficient programs that avoid unnecessary memory consumption and potential memory leaks.
